name: Git and code reviews
note: Questions authored by Claude as practice material. Not sourced from your own notes or any official exam. Verify anything you doubt against the docs.

questions.q: Which command replays your feature-branch commits on top of the latest main?
questions.why: Rebase moves your commits onto the new base and keeps history linear; merge adds a merge commit.

questions.q: You hit conflicts during a rebase and fixed the files. What comes next?
questions.why: Stage the resolved files, then continue the rebase.

questions.q: Undo the last commit but keep its changes staged. Which command?
questions.why: --soft moves the branch back and leaves changes staged. --hard would discard them.

questions.q: You need one specific commit from another branch on your branch. Which command?
questions.why: Cherry-pick applies a single commit as a new commit.

questions.q: Why should you avoid rebasing and force-pushing a branch others already pulled?
options: It rewrites history their work is based on
questions.why: Rewritten commits get new hashes, so teammates' copies diverge.

questions.q: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
options: fetch downloads changes without merging; pull fetches then merges or rebases
questions.why: git pull = git fetch + merge (or rebase).

questions.q: Which is the safer way to force-push after a rebase?
questions.why: --force-with-lease refuses to overwrite remote commits you have not seen.

questions.q: Which review comment is most useful on a test PR?
options: This test still passes if the API returns 500 because the status is never asserted. Assert 200 and check the body.
I would have written it differently
questions.why: It names the problem, the risk and a concrete fix.

questions.q: What does git stash do?
options: Shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch branches cleanly
questions.why: Stash saves working changes aside; git stash pop restores them.

questions.q: Why prefer git revert over git reset on a shared branch?
options: revert adds a new commit that undoes a change, so history is not rewritten
questions.why: Revert is safe for shared history.

questions.q: What does git init do?
options: Creates a new empty repository in the current folder
questions.why: It creates the .git directory that tracks the project.

questions.q: What does git status show?
options: Which files are modified, staged or untracked
questions.why: It summarises working tree and staging area.

questions.q: What does git clone do?
options: Copies a remote repository to your machine, with history
questions.why: Clone fetches the full repo and sets origin.

questions.q: What does git add do?
options: Stages changes for the next commit
questions.why: Staging chooses what goes into the next commit.

questions.q: What does git log --oneline show?
options: A compact list, one line per commit
questions.why: Short hash plus the message for each commit.

questions.q: What is .gitignore for?
options: Lists files and patterns Git should not track
questions.why: Use it for build output, node_modules, local env files.

questions.q: How does the result of merge differ from rebase for a feature branch?
options: Merge keeps both histories with a merge commit; rebase gives a linear history
Rebase keeps merge commits; merge is linear
questions.why: They integrate the same changes but shape history differently.

questions.q: What does git diff --staged show?
options: Changes staged for the next commit compared with the last commit
questions.why: It is a preview of what the next commit will contain.

questions.q: What does git commit --amend do?
options: Replaces the last commit with a new one, with new content or message
Deletes the last commit and its changes
questions.why: It rewrites the last commit, so avoid it once pushed and shared.

questions.q: What is a fast-forward merge?
options: The branch pointer simply moves ahead because there is no divergent work
questions.why: No merge commit is needed when the target has not moved.

questions.q: In a conflict, what sits between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======?
options: The version from your current branch
questions.why: Between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming change.

questions.q: Which PR habit helps reviewers most?
options: Small focused PRs with a clear description
questions.why: Small PRs get faster and better reviews.

questions.q: You hard-reset and lost commits. Which command helps you find them?
questions.why: Reflog records where HEAD has been, so lost commits can be recovered.

questions.q: In git rebase -i, which action melds a commit into the previous one and discards its message?
questions.why: fixup keeps the previous message; squash lets you combine messages.

questions.q: What does git merge --no-ff do?
options: Creates a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible
questions.why: It preserves the fact that a branch existed.

questions.q: What is git worktree useful for?
options: Checking out several branches at once in separate folders from one repository
questions.why: It avoids stashing when switching context.

questions.q: To revert a merge commit you must pass -m 1. Why?
options: To say which parent line is the mainline to keep
questions.why: A merge has two parents, so Git needs to know which side to keep.

questions.q: What does git pull --rebase do compared with a plain pull?
options: Replays your local commits on top of the fetched ones instead of making a merge commit
questions.why: It keeps history linear when you pull.

questions.q: When reviewing a new test, which check best shows it is meaningful?
options: Break the code under test on purpose and confirm the test fails
questions.why: A test that cannot fail proves nothing.

questions.q: You committed while in a detached HEAD. How do you keep the work?
options: Create a branch there, for example git switch -c rescue
questions.why: Commits on a detached HEAD can be lost once you switch away.
